html:
A carved granite stele about 24 metres tall, made in the 4th century CE in the city of Aksum, in northern Ethiopia. It was taken to Rome in 1937 and returned in 2005.

The kings of Aksum marked their tombs with tall stone stelae. The finest are carved to look like many storeyed buildings, with false doors at the base and rows of windows above, copying Aksum's own houses of wood and stone. This one weighs about 160 tonnes. An even bigger stele lies broken nearby.

After Mussolini's army conquered Ethiopia in the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, Italian soldiers took the stele, which was lying in pieces, to Rome. It was set up in 1937 as a trophy of the new empire.

Italy promised in 1947 to give it back but delayed for decades. In 2005 it was finally flown home in three pieces and re-erected in 2008. The stelae of Aksum belong to the time before Aksum adopted Christianity, after which churches took the place of tombs as royal monuments.
sum: A carved granite stele about 24 metres tall, made in the 4th century CE in the city of Aksum, in northern Ethiopia. It was taken to Rome in 1937 and returned in 2005.
